label: TICKET-1031
raw_text: checkout-frontend: A customer submitted a support ticket saying the 'Add to Cart' button on the product page added the item twice when they tapped it once on their phone. Screenshot shows quantity: 2 for a single tap. Conditions: mobile device, tapped once but screen was slow to respond so user may have tapped again without realizing

extraction.symptom_summary: Add to Cart button registers two items after a single tap on mobile
extraction.conditions: mobile device; UI response lag causing user to possibly tap again quickly
extraction.frequency_pattern: appears when the screen is slow to respond, leading to duplicate addition; not reported as constant
mechanism_hypotheses: event handler invoked twice due to race condition
state update race causing duplicate write
extraction.recall_query: single tap on a button results in duplicate action, often when UI latency causes rapid re‑tap, leading to two items being added instead of one

verdict.mechanism_reasoning: All three past tickets involve a race condition where a debounce guard is set asynchronously (via React state), allowing rapid successive taps to invoke the same handler twice. The new bug shows duplicate Add‑to‑Cart actions after a single tap on a slow‑responding mobile UI, matching the same missing/ineffective debounce mechanism.
verdict.why_symptoms_look_different: Earlier incidents manifested as a UI hang (TICKET-1001) or duplicate order creation/payment authorizations (TICKET-1042, TICKET-1108). This bug appears as duplicate items in the cart, but the underlying double‑submission race caused by UI lag and insufficient debouncing is the same.
verdict.past_fix_assessment: The fixes applied previously were workarounds (increased debounce timeout, loading spinners, backend idempotency keys) and do not eliminate the root cause of the asynchronous debounce guard, so the underlying race condition likely remains.
verdict.likely_root_cause: Missing or ineffective debounce guard on the Add‑to‑Cart tap handler, causing a race where the guard flag is set after the handler has already been invoked, allowing two submissions when the UI is slow.
verdict.recommended_action: Implement a robust, synchronous debounce/throttle on the Add‑to‑Cart button (set guard flag before any async work and clear it only after request completion). Add backend idempotency (e.g., a unique cart‑add token) to reject duplicate adds within a short window. Update the UI to display a loading state that blocks further taps until the request resolves.
evidence_gaps: No server logs confirming that two separate add‑to‑Cart requests were received.
No stack trace or code snippet showing the current tap handler implementation.
Unclear whether any backend idempotency already exists for cart modifications.

label: TICKET-2201
raw_text: wishlist-service: Customer emailed support confused because they deleted an item from their wishlist yesterday but it 'came back' when they checked today on a different device. Conditions: cross-device sync, same shared CDN/edge cache infra

extraction.symptom_summary: Deleted wishlist item reappears when viewed on another device after sync
extraction.conditions: cross-device sync; shared CDN/edge cache infrastructure
mechanism_hypotheses: stale CDN cache causing outdated data to be served
eventual consistency delay between storage and cache
race condition where concurrent writes overwrite delete
extraction.recall_query: wishlist item deletion does not persist across devices, causing the item to reappear after synchronization

verdict.mechanism_reasoning: Both incidents stem from a missing concurrency control mechanism. In TICKET-5103 the lack of optimistic locking caused concurrent admin edits to silently overwrite each other (last‑write‑wins). The new wishlist bug is hypothesized to involve a race where a delete operation is overwritten by a concurrent update from another device, leading to the deleted item reappearing. The underlying root‑cause mechanism—absence of version checks/optimistic locking resulting in lost updates—is the same.
verdict.why_symptoms_look_different: The domains differ: one is an admin dashboard editing customer records, the other is a cross‑device wishlist sync. Consequently the user‑visible symptom is an overwritten record versus a resurrected wishlist item, but both are manifestations of the same lost‑update race condition.
verdict.past_fix_assessment: The fix for TICKET-5103 introduced optimistic locking with a version field, eliminating the last‑write‑wins problem. Since the root cause was addressed, applying a similar concurrency‑control fix to the wishlist service should resolve the issue.
verdict.likely_root_cause: Missing optimistic locking or version check on wishlist item updates, allowing concurrent writes to overwrite a delete operation.
verdict.recommended_action: Review the wishlist-service update path for concurrent operations. Add a version field or compare‑and‑set logic to enforce optimistic locking. Ensure delete operations invalidate or update any CDN/edge cache entries atomically. Add conflict detection and retry logic for concurrent updates. Deploy tests that simulate cross‑device concurrent modifications to verify the fix.
evidence_gaps: No logs or timestamps showing concurrent update/delete events.
Unclear whether the CDN cache is actually serving stale data or if the race condition is the primary cause.
No details on current concurrency control mechanisms (if any) used by wishlist-service.

label: TICKET-3142
raw_text: calendar-integration: A user in Sydney says a meeting they scheduled for 9am shows up as 9am the previous day in their synced calendar app. Conditions: timezone far ahead of UTC, calendar sync feature

extraction.symptom_summary: Meeting scheduled for 9 am appears as 9 am the previous day in the synced calendar
extraction.conditions: User in a timezone far ahead of UTC (e.g., Sydney) using the calendar sync feature
extraction.recall_query: Meeting times displayed a day earlier in synced calendars for users in far‑ahead timezones during calendar synchronization

verdict.mechanism_reasoning: All three incidents stem from the same underlying mechanism: incorrect handling of timezone offsets when converting timestamps for user‑facing output. In the new bug the calendar sync converts a UTC timestamp to the user's local time incorrectly, causing a one‑day shift for users far ahead of UTC. TICKET-3011 and TICKET-3054 exhibit the identical flaw—using server‑local time or a hard‑coded offset instead of a proper per‑user timezone conversion—resulting in dates being off by a day at midnight boundaries.
verdict.why_symptoms_look_different: The components differ (calendar‑integration vs billing‑service vs analytics‑service) and the user‑visible artifacts are distinct (calendar event vs invoice date vs usage report), but the root cause is the same timezone conversion error.
verdict.past_fix_assessment: Both past fixes were workarounds (hard‑coded offset adjustment and manual query range tweak) that do not address the fundamental timezone handling logic, so the underlying bug likely remains.
verdict.likely_root_cause: Timezone conversion logic that assumes server‑local time or applies a static offset instead of converting UTC timestamps to the user's stored timezone, leading to off‑by‑one‑day errors for users in far‑ahead timezones.
verdict.recommended_action: Replace the ad‑hoc timezone handling with a robust, timezone‑aware library (e.g., java.time, moment.js, date‑fns). Store all timestamps in UTC and convert to the user's timezone only at presentation. Add comprehensive unit and integration tests covering edge cases around midnight and DST transitions. Conduct a code‑base audit to find and fix similar patterns in other services.
evidence_gaps: No code snippet showing how the calendar‑integration performs the conversion.
No logs or stack trace confirming the exact point of failure.
Unclear whether timestamps are stored in UTC or already localized before sync.

label: TICKET-4132
raw_text: notifications-worker: notifications-worker pod got OOM-killed twice last night. Memory usage graph shows a steady climb over about 60 hours before the crash. Conditions: long-running worker process, no traffic-based pattern (background job, not request-driven)

extraction.symptom_summary: notifications-worker pod was OOM‑killed after memory usage steadily increased over about 60 hours
extraction.conditions: long-running worker process, background job, not request‑driven
extraction.recall_query: OOM kill of a long‑running background worker after a gradual memory climb over many hours

verdict.mechanism_reasoning: Both incidents are caused by a resource‑leak pattern: the past ticket leaked database connections, exhausting the connection pool and causing 502 errors; the new bug shows a steady memory increase leading to OOM, which is a memory‑leak variant of the same underlying failure mechanism – code that fails to release or bound a resource over time.
verdict.why_symptoms_look_different: The leaked resource differs (DB connections vs heap memory), so the observable failure differs (intermittent 502 errors that disappear after a pod restart vs a pod being OOM‑killed after many hours). The timing and symptom class also differ because memory exhaustion manifests as a crash, whereas connection exhaustion manifests as request failures.
verdict.past_fix_assessment: The past fix for TICKET-4077 was a workaround (restart the pod). The underlying connection‑leak bug likely remains, indicating the root‑cause pattern (missing release of resources) is still present in the codebase.
verdict.likely_root_cause: A memory leak in the notifications‑worker process, possibly due to an unbounded queue, cache, or other data structure that grows over time without proper cleanup.
verdict.recommended_action: 1. Add detailed memory profiling (heap dumps, pprof) to pinpoint the growing allocation. 2. Review recent code changes for unbounded collections, long‑lived goroutines, or caches that are not evicted. 3. Implement bounds or eviction policies for queues/caches. 4. Add alerts on sustained memory growth and consider a graceful pod restart policy as a temporary mitigation. 5. Deploy a fix that ensures all allocated resources are released or bounded.
evidence_gaps: No stack trace or heap dump provided.
No logs indicating which functions were executing during the memory increase.
No information about recent code deployments or library updates.
Unclear whether any external libraries used in the worker have known memory‑leak issues.
